title: Energy stocks: how to analyze oil, power and the transition
description: Energy stocks: commodity price, heavy investment and the energy transition. The business models, key ratios and a five-step checklist — with sources.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Energy stocks are shares in companies that earn money by finding, producing, transporting or selling energy — oil, natural gas, electricity and renewable sources. Nearly all share two traits: the commodity price is set on a global market no single company controls, and the business is capital-intensive: platforms, grids and power plants cost billions before the first revenue lands. That is why analyzing energy stocks looks different from analyzing, say, a software company — different, not harder.

This guide walks through the business models, the prices that steer earnings, the ratios that matter most and the transition's two parallel playing fields — and ends with a five-step checklist. With sources for anyone who wants to read on.

## Three kinds of energy stocks — drillers, chains and power companies

The first group is the exploration and production companies, often called upstream: they locate and produce oil and gas. Revenue is essentially volume times commodity price, minus a cost structure that is mostly fixed. In AK1A's company universe, Equinor, Aker BP and Vår Energi are examples — their results swing directly with the oil and gas price.

The second group is the integrated majors — Chevron, ExxonMobil and Shell — which own the entire chain: exploration, refineries, tankers and stations. That makes earnings less one-sided: when the price of crude oil and finished products moves differently, the refining margin can carry the year when production disappoints, and the other way around.

The third group is the power and renewable companies — Iberdrola, Enel, RWE and Fortum. Their revenue comes from power generation and regulated grids, where the grid business often has a return set by regulators while the power plants' earnings follow the electricity price. Three groups, three revenue machines — and the analysis always begins with determining which of them a company actually runs.

## The price on top of the company — the commodity steers earnings

For the upstream company the commodity price is the single biggest variable, and it swings hard: Brent crude traded below 20 dollars per barrel during the pandemic in 2020 and above 120 dollars per barrel two years later (EIA). The leverage is mechanical: the costs of keeping production running are essentially the same at 40 and 80 dollars.

An example of what is called operating leverage: a producer with a breakeven point of 50 dollars per barrel that sees the price 80 earns 30 dollars per barrel in margin. If the price falls by a third, to 53 dollars, the margin falls by more than 80 percent — to 3 dollars per barrel. The price move is moderate; the earnings move is not.

For the power companies the mechanism is the same, but the market is another. The electricity price is formed on the European power exchange Nord Pool, per bidding zone — in Sweden SE1 to SE4 — and swings with hydro reservoirs, wind, temperature and transmission capacity. A precipitation-rich year gives low prices; a cold and wind-poor one gives high. On top of this a currency leg: oil is priced in dollars, so earnings move with both the commodity price and the dollar rate.

## The ratios that matter most in energy stocks

Because the plants are expensive, depreciation becomes large, and earnings after depreciation can give a skewed picture of the cash flow. That is why EBITDA and EV/EBITDA are the standard measures of the sector — the entire capital structure is set in relation to operating earnings before depreciation. How to calculate it is in the course [EV/EBIT](/kurser/km-010-evebit), and the background in [What is EV/EBITDA?](/blogg/vad-ar-ev-ebitda).

Next: capital expenditures. An energy company can show strong earnings and at the same time build away its free cash flow in new projects — [cash flow analysis](/kurser/km-003-kassaflodesanalysen) is therefore at least as important as the income statement. Debt reads best as net debt through EBITDA — how many years of current cash flow the debt corresponds to; deeper in [Debt-to-equity: what level is dangerous?](/blogg/skuldsattningsgrad-vilken-niva-ar-farlig).

For the upstream companies two sector-specific questions are added: reserves and reserve replacement. The reserves are the volumes of oil and gas the company can produce with reasonable certainty; the reserve replacement ratio shows whether it each year replaces what it produces. If reserves are produced out without replacement, the future revenue base shrinks — even when this year's report looks strong.

Finally the dividend: many energy companies have dividend decisions directly tied to the commodity price, which makes the dividend predictable but also price-sensitive. And the cycle trap that always applies to the P/E ratio is extra sharp here — a low P/E at a price peak is rarely a real discount. That craft is built in [the P/E deep dive](/kurser/km-009-pe).

## The energy transition — two playing fields at once

The sector is analyzed today against an upheaval in full swing. According to the IEA's World Energy Investment 2026, global energy investment is expected to reach 3,400 billion dollars during the year, of which 2,200 billion — almost twice as much as the fossil investment — goes to clean energy: solar, wind, grids, nuclear and electric cars.

For the analysis this means the sector houses two business logics at once. The fossil-dominated companies are valued on how long oil and gas demand carries them — and on the risk that resources and plants lose their value earlier than calculated: transition risk. The renewable companies are valued on growth: order backlogs, project management and long-term power contracts — especially fixed-price agreements with solid counterparties — make their revenue less commodity-bound. Regulation, from concessions and grid tariffs to subsidies and auctions, is a decisive variable on both sides; those mechanisms are covered in [Regulatory risk](/blogg/v18-regulatoriska-analys).

## How to analyze energy stocks — a five-step checklist

1. **Map the revenue model.** Volume times price, fee base or regulated grid business? The answer determines which ratios are relevant.
2. **Read the cash flow before the earnings.** Capital expenditures against depreciation: is the company building value, or are the projects eating the cash flow?
3. **Set the ratios against the sector.** EV/EBITDA and net debt/EBITDA are compared with the company's own history and the sector median — see [sector medians from AKM2](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2).
4. **Test the price sensitivity.** Which commodity price gives the breakeven point? How does the dividend move if the price falls 20 percent?
5. **Place the company in the energy transition.** Share of revenue from renewables and grids, verifiable transition targets, regulatory exposure.

The routine is the method: the same five steps every quarter, together with [the reading order of the quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten) and the overall methodology in [the complete guide to Swedish equity analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026).

## Three mistakes worth untangling

- **Low P/E as a real discount.** At a cycle peak the earnings are at their highest exactly when the multiple looks lowest — the same trap as in all cyclical industries, but sharper here.
- **Seeing the sector as a single bet.** The correlation between energy stocks is high, but a regulated grid and an exploration company have different revenue machines — measure the co-movement instead of assuming it ([Correlation and diversification](/kurser/km-014-korrelation-diversifiering)).
- **Ignoring currency and commodity quality.** Oil is priced in dollars, and different crude grades and gas markets give different prices to different companies — small input differences give large differences in the conclusion.

## The summary

- Energy stocks divide into three revenue machines: exploration and production, integrated chains, and power and grids.
- The commodity price is the biggest variable, and operating leverage amplifies price moves into earnings moves — in the example the margin fell by more than 80 percent on a price drop of a third.
- The sector's key ratios are EV/EBITDA, capital expenditures, net debt/EBITDA, reserves and the dividend's price sensitivity.
- The energy transition makes the sector two playing fields: a demand horizon for fossil, growth and regulation for renewables.
- The analysis always begins with the revenue model — the checklist's five steps are the working order.
